newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW - Canada July CPI up 1.8 pct on year.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Canada July CPI up 1.8 pct on year.

text.p: Following are reactions to consumer price index data released by Statistics Canada on Tuesday.
Canada's unadjusted July consumer price index was unchanged in the month and rose 1.8 percent in the year, Statistics Canada said Tuesday. Core CPI rose 1.5 percent year-on-year.

Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast, on average, that unadjusted CPI would rise 0.1 percent on the month. The survey forecast a 1.8 percent year-over-year rise in the all-items index and a 1.9 percent rise in core CPI.

Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs. "The numbers are good on the face of it. The surprise came in the core CPI number. We were looking at 1.7 percent and it came in at 1.5 percent. The reaction will be positive on the markets. What this does is, it delays the immediate need for a rate hike from the Bank of Canada."

Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers. "The numbers are a little bit better than expected and it shows that there are very few inflationary pressures in the economy. The market will continue to push back the timing for any prospective Bank of Canada rate hike, and I think the one casualty will be the Canadian dollar, which will take it a bit on the nose today."

Andrew Pyle, economist with ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett. "It's going to be slightly negative for the currency. Directly, it's a positive for fixed-income markets because it gives people one more reason to believe the Bank of Canada will not tighten. That very reason is why we will see a slightly negative hit on the currency."

Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist with the Bank of Montreal. "They're pretty encouraging, especially when you look at the core rate dropping to 1.5 percent from 2.0 percent. There is an indication that continuing slack in the economy is putting downward pressure on prices. The Bank of Canada is still probably more focused on growth, and if they get indications later this month of strength in the second quarter and continuing into the third, they could tighten policy gradually."
